questions.title: Does La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) require a human signature to "certify" a cancellation request?
questions.question_body: The statute says the premium finance company must send a copy of the notice of cancellation "together with a statement certifying" items (i)–(iv), but it never mentions a signature. Plaintiffs argued that "certifying" implies a signed attestation before cancellation. The Fifth Circuit held no signature is required, distinguishing Benitez v. Elsayed because there the notice didn't purport to certify at all. Under Louisiana law, can a corporation "certify" via an unsigned document or automated email that states "APAC certifies..." without any individual's name or signature? Are there Louisiana authorities (statutes, UETA, evidence rules) that define certification in a way that would require a signature or identifiable affiant?

questions.title: What qualifies as "receipt" by the insurer under § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i) — is an automated web service/email sufficient?
questions.question_body: The statute says that upon "receipt" of the finance company's notice and certification, the insurer may proceed to cancel. Here, GoAuto's system auto-cancelled when an APAC system emailed and/or pinged a GoAuto web service in the early morning, before any human at GoAuto touched the paperwork. The court relied on Black's definitions and treated the computer's intake as "receipt." Is there Louisiana authority on whether electronic delivery to an automated system constitutes the insurer's receipt for statutory purposes? Would it matter if the 'receipt' was through an API/web service call rather than traditional email? And does it matter that a human only stamps the paper later in the morning?

questions.title: How does the "strict adherence" requirement square with the court’s refusal to add a signature requirement not in the text?
questions.question_body: Louisiana courts demand "strict adherence" to § 9:3550 when a finance company cancels under a power of attorney, and any defect invalidates cancellation. Plaintiffs argued that strict adherence means insisting on a signature and other formalities to fix timing and ensure accuracy. The Fifth Circuit responded that strict adherence isn't an invitation to add requirements not in the statute. Do Louisiana cases define 'strict adherence' as compliance with the express text only, or do they sometimes infer procedural safeguards (like signatures or named preparers) from terms such as 'certifying'? How do cases like Delatte, Eaglin, Britten, and Benitez frame the line between strict textual compliance and judicially implied formalities?

questions.title: Can hand-delivery by an affiliate’s or the finance company’s employee qualify as delivery "with a private carrier" under § 9:3550(G)(3)(a)?
questions.question_body: The district court floated an alternative ground that the APAC employee who physically delivered/stamped the notices was a 'private carrier' under the statute, but the Fifth Circuit called that rationale 'imaginative and unconventional' and didn't reach it. Is there any Louisiana authority defining 'private carrier' in this statutory context? In practice, would hand-delivery by an employee of the finance company (or an affiliate) count as delivery 'with a private carrier,' or does 'private carrier' imply an independent third-party delivery service? If the email route failed, would placing the documents in a shared filing cabinet controlled by a related management company constitute either 'private carrier' delivery or 'receipt' by the insurer?

questions.title: Does § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i)’s "insurer may proceed to cancel" language permit immediate, automated cancellation, or does it require a discretionary human act?
questions.question_body: The insurer 'may proceed to cancel' upon receipt of the compliant notice and certification. GoAuto’s system automatically cancels at the moment of electronic receipt (after the 10-day cure period expires). Is that consistent with the statute’s use of 'may' (suggesting discretion) and the purpose of fixing the exact date/time of cancellation? Is there any Louisiana case law on whether the insurer must make a contemporaneous, discretionary decision after receipt, or whether pre-programmed automated cancellation upon receipt is permissible?

questions.title: Why did the court’s finding of statutory compliance dispose of the misrepresentation and good-faith claims with prejudice?
questions.question_body: The plaintiffs (including a third-party accident victim, Jenkins) alleged misrepresentations and breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing. The Fifth Circuit affirms dismissal of all claims after concluding GoAuto’s cancellation procedures complied with § 9:3550. Are these tort/bad-faith theories in Louisiana entirely derivative of an ineffective cancellation (i.e., if cancellation is valid, the claims necessarily fail)? Could an insured or third party still have a viable claim based on how cancellation was communicated or recorded even if the cancellation itself was effective? How does Jenkins, as a non-insured injured by a GoAuto insured whose policy was canceled, have standing or a cause of action tied to alleged cancellation defects?

questions.title: When will the Fifth Circuit certify unsettled Louisiana-law questions, and did it make an Erie guess here?
questions.question_body: Plaintiffs asked the court to certify the meaning of 'certifying' and 'receipt' to the Louisiana Supreme Court, arguing industry-wide importance. The Fifth Circuit declined, citing Jefferson v. Lead Industries, and proceeded to rely on Black’s Law Dictionary and intermediate appellate decisions (KMJ Services, Hodges, Lewis, Benitez). Under Erie, how does the Fifth Circuit weigh Louisiana intermediate appellate decisions and secondary sources when the Louisiana Supreme Court hasn't spoken? What factors make a 'compelling reason' for certification, and why didn't the court find one here despite the lack of controlling authority and the strict-adherence doctrine?
